guide.title: What is programming?
guide.text: Programming means describing a task with precise instructions. The computer follows the language rules; it does not guess your intention.
guide.takeaway: Here the goal is to display 7. Change the number and the displayed result changes.

guide.title: From text to action
guide.text: A compiler analyses text and translates it into a form a runtime can execute. This game's small interpreter first builds a structure, then evaluates it.
guide.takeaway: Meaning comes from structure: add first, then display. This game does not run the full Tolang compilation pipeline.

guide.title: Mistakes are clues
guide.text: Syntax rules describe valid shapes. A missing parenthesis breaks that shape. A valid program can still do the wrong thing: displaying 8 is valid, but it does not meet a goal of 9.
guide.takeaway: First make the program valid, then check whether its actual result meets the task.

guide.title: Why count work?
guide.text: Different instructions can produce the same result with different amounts of work. Computing and storing data use resources. The step count here is only a model for learning.
guide.takeaway: Both display 5. The second needs an addition. These counts cannot predict TVM gas or transaction fees.

guide.title: Tolang and a blockchain
guide.text: Tolang is used to write programs for ALUX. On a blockchain, changing shared state also involves transaction rules and agreement between nodes. Language and execution environment both matter.
guide.takeaway: Displaying a number in this game sends no blockchain transaction. These first ideas also help you learn other programming languages.

guide.title: Choose and repeat
guide.text: A comparison produces true or false. if chooses a branch; for traverses a list or range, and while repeats while its condition is true. Tolang’s and and or evaluate both sides, so they do not protect a division by zero on the other side.
guide.takeaway: Predict both the displayed values and the number of outputs. A different iteration count can change a movement plan.

guide.title: Return a value or reply
guide.text: sync fn with return value produces a call-stack result. return ! value sends a function reply. Write the return explicitly: a function does not automatically return its last expression. A missing reply can leave its caller waiting.
guide.takeaway: Fewer arguments can create a partially applied function. Too many arguments do not create extra parameters.

guide.title: Coordinate messages
guide.text: let parcel; creates a communication name. ! sends and ? receives. A joint receive uses & to wait until all matching messages are available. | composes concurrent work; its appearance does not promise which output comes first.
guide.code:
let a; let b;
{ a ! 4 | b ! 6 | ?(x <- a & y <- b) { (x + y).log() } }
guide.takeaway: If one message is missing, the receive stays waiting. Use a joint receive when later work requires both values.

chase.title: Starport Chase
chase.intro: Be the police or the thief. Read the street, write a plan and watch every signal change the chase.
chase.policeGoal: Catch the thief before the exit
chase.thiefGoal: Reach the exit before you are caught
chase.rules: You move first, then your rival moves one space. Land on a roadblock and you stay put, but your rival still moves. You can jump over a roadblock. The thief escapes at space 18; the police catch them by reaching or passing their position.
chase.clue: Look at the numbered positions. Plan the landing spots, not just the total distance.
chase.signalRule: Each output must be an integer from 1 to 3: the number of spaces you move. Print 1–8 signals in order. A chase ends as soon as someone is caught or escapes; later signals are not used.
chase.keyboard: Write the code here, then run it. Typing speed does not change the chase.
chase.ready: The street is waiting for your plan.
chase.changed: Plan changed. Run it again to see what happens.
chase.retry: Trace each landing and try another plan. Retrying costs nothing.
chase.meaning: let gives a value a name; + adds values; .log() prints a value. This game reads each printed number as a move. The same code can control different things in another game.
chase.local: Both roles’ drafts and completed districts stay in this browser. Login does not sync them. These missions are untimed.

dispatch.title: Starport Dispatch
dispatch.intro: Write a program that handles every delivery batch. Watch what it sends, compare the results and adjust your plan.
dispatch.entry: Route cargo with conditions, loops, functions and cooperating messages. New rounds bring new dispatch data.

missions.title: Choose a dock
missions.brief: Send signal 1 when cargo is below threshold; otherwise send signal 2. Each batch needs exactly one signal.
missions.hint: Compare cargo with threshold in if. Check the batch where cargo equals threshold as well as the batches on either side.
missions.learned: Your condition routes different loads without changing the program.

missions.title: Follow the manifest
missions.brief: Use for to read docks in order. Add offset to each dock number and display the new destination. An empty manifest needs no signals.
missions.hint: Use the current loop item in the addition. Repeated dock numbers still represent separate deliveries.
missions.learned: Your loop handles empty, short and repeated manifests in order.

missions.title: Calculate fuel
missions.brief: Define fuel(cargo, reserve) and return the sum of its two parameters. The station calls your function with different cargo loads and reserves, then displays its return value. Your code only needs the function definition.
missions.hint: Use an explicit return. Choose your own parameter names, but keep the function name fuel so the station can call it. You do not need .log() here.
missions.learned: One reusable function calculates fuel for different cargo loads and reserves.

missions.title: Combine the reports
missions.brief: The station sends reports through west and east. Receive both together and combine their received values in a sync function. If the total exceeds threshold, add reserve. Display only the resulting total.
missions.hint: Use & for the joint receive. Both received values must reach your function result, and that result must reach the displayed calculation.
missions.learned: Messages, a function and a condition now cooperate across different reports.

guideStudio.title: Change a line. See what happens.
guideStudio.intro: Predict, then run. Each value your program logs appears on a beacon in front of you.
guideStudio.compareIntro: Start with a familiar concept, compare the code, then run the Tolang example. Messages and replies deserve a closer look.
guideStudio.sceneRule: Each log entry lights one beacon
guideStudio.ready: The desk is ready. Run the code and see what arrives.
guideStudio.noOutput: The program finished without output. Try adding .log().
guideStudio.comparisonScope: These examples produce the same simple numeric results. Only Tolang runs here. Matching results do not mean identical types, scheduling or execution models.
guideStudio.messageDifference: Tolang message sends, receives, joins and function replies have no single word-for-word replacement across Python, JavaScript and Rust. Run the Tolang example above, then explore real data dependencies in a coordination task.
guideStudio.transfer: Try new inputs at Starport Dispatch

stations.title: Output
stations.prompt: Send a number to the desk. Predict what 7.log() will produce.
stations.try: Replace 7 with a number of your own, then run again. What changes?
stations.meaning: .log() writes this value to the log. Beacons display the log here; logging does not automatically move a character.
stations.difference: Python uses print, JavaScript often uses console.log, and Rust often uses println!. Matching results do not make these the same calling mechanism.

stations.title: Calculation
stations.prompt: Two supply loads contain 2 and 3 units. Add them before sending the total.
stations.try: Change just one number to make the total 9.
stations.meaning: The expression inside the parentheses is evaluated before its result is logged.
stations.difference: These small integer additions produce the same result. Large numbers, type conversion and overflow have separate rules in each language.

stations.title: Names
stations.prompt: Name a supply load n, then calculate the total after adding two units.
stations.try: Change the value bound to n and observe the new output.
stations.meaning: A name lets later expressions refer to a value. Editing invalidates the old output; run again to see the new result.
stations.difference: Python assigns directly; these JavaScript and Tolang examples use let. Rust let bindings are immutable by default. Similar spelling does not imply identical binding rules.

stations.title: Choice
stations.prompt: With fuel above 4, signal beacon 1. Otherwise signal beacon 2.
stations.try: Set fuel to 4, then to 5. Which branch runs at the boundary?
stations.meaning: if selects a branch using a condition. Only the selected branch logs a value here.
stations.difference: The Tolang example requires then. Python uses indentation; JavaScript and Rust use braces. Rust requires a boolean condition.

stations.title: Repetition
stations.prompt: Signal beacons 2, 4 and 6 in order. Predict whether there will be one output or three.
stations.try: Add a number to the list, then use the arrows to inspect each output.
stations.meaning: for takes successive values from the list. The same output expression executes repeatedly, so the highlight points to the same code.
stations.difference: All three examples iterate over integer lists. JavaScript for...of iterates over values, unlike for...in. Collection and ownership rules still differ.

stations.title: Functions
stations.prompt: Name a way to combine two loads, then call it with 3 and 4.
stations.try: Change one argument so that the result becomes 10.
stations.meaning: This example uses sync fn and an ordinary return to pass a computed value to its caller before logging it.
stations.difference: This Tolang function is synchronous. Rust declares parameter and return types and can use a tail expression. Python and JavaScript use ordinary return here. Tolang return ! is different.

stations.title: Replies
stations.prompt: Compare this with the previous station: return ! sends a reply, and later statements can still execute.
stations.try: Change the reply value and inspect the log, then distinguish replies from output in the independent task.
stations.meaning: Returning from a function and sending a reply are different actions. Replacing a reply with an ordinary return changes the meaning.
stations.difference: Tolang return ! can continue after sending a reply; ordinary return exits the function. A JavaScript Promise or Rust Future is not a direct equivalent.

stations.title: Coordination
stations.prompt: Two reports arrive on separate channels. A join waits for both values before combining them.
stations.try: Change the value in one message and check that it contributes to the total.
stations.meaning: The combining action needs data from both receives. The order shown here does not represent every possible concurrent schedule.
stations.difference: Message concurrency differs from ordinary sequential calls. Channels, queues, threads and async scheduling need separate treatment. The same total does not prove equivalent concurrent behavior.

pursuit.title: Continuous pursuit
pursuit.intro: Run, choose routes and clear roadblocks. A whole-match result requires at least ten minutes, followed by a real interception or escape.
pursuit.controls: Space to jump; hold Shift to sprint. Route choices apply when entering the next road section.

pursuit.strategyNote: The program reads current energy, obstacle, gap, round and rivalEnergy. Each output lasts 250 milliseconds. When the queue empties, the same program runs again with fresh world inputs.
pursuit.signals: Output 1 to keep pace, 2 to sprint, or 3 to attempt a jump. Each run must output 1–8 signals and cannot remain waiting for messages.
pursuit.idlePlan: Deploy to see the actual execution result.
pursuit.caught: The police caught the thief at their actual positions.
pursuit.saveChoice: Pursuit keeps the selected version as a whole, including the current scene and match history. Progress from the two versions is not combined.
pursuit.resultNote: Review routes, collisions and energy, then try another strategy. Match results are not programming grades.

pursuit.artError: The street art could not load. Reopen this page to retry.
pursuit.rules: Two roads meet at their far ends. Police arriving first backtrack along the escape road to intercept. Equal progress on different streets or branches is not contact. Energy, jumps and earlier mistakes affect the rest of the match. Pausing, background time, code editing and replay do not count as active time.
pursuit.minimum: At least 10 minutes; the clock alone never decides the result.
pursuit.savedPaused: Scene restored. Time advances only after you resume.

names.title: Names and arithmetic
names.goal: Add the inputs cargo and reserve, then output their sum. Your program must work when the inputs change.
names.context: The task supplies cargo and reserve. Write the calculation and output.
names.hint: Use the input names instead of a fixed answer for one case. You can call .log() on a parenthesized sum.

branch.title: Choosing a branch
branch.goal: Output 1 when fuel is greater than threshold. Output 2 when it is equal or smaller.
branch.context: The task supplies fuel and threshold, including values exactly on the boundary.
branch.hint: Compare the values, then use if to select one branch. Which branch should equality take?

repeat.title: A changing list
repeat.goal: Follow the order of docks and output each entry plus offset. An empty list produces no output.
repeat.context: The task supplies a list named docks and a number named offset. Entries may repeat or be negative.
repeat.hint: Use for to read each entry, then add to that entry. Do not fix the number of outputs.

counter.title: A changing counter
counter.goal: Use while to output a counter starting at 0, increasing by 1 and stopping before limit. When limit is 0, output nothing.
counter.context: The task supplies limit. Create and update your own counter in the program.
counter.hint: Choose an initial counter value, compare it with limit, and advance it at the end of each iteration.

function.title: Function returns
function.goal: Define combine with two parameters and return their sum through a synchronous function. The task calls it and displays the returned value.
function.context: The call is combine(firstNumber, secondNumber). You may choose your parameter names; you do not need to add .log().
function.hint: Return the sum with an ordinary return. The task uses the returned value, not an extra print inside the function.

reply.title: Function replies
reply.goal: Define boost with two parameters and reply with their sum using return !. The task waits for the reply and displays it.
reply.context: The call is boost(firstNumber, secondNumber). You may choose your parameter names; you do not need to add .log().
reply.hint: An explicit fn reply uses return !. This area checks the reply mechanism rather than an ordinary synchronous return.

message.title: Receiving a message
message.goal: Receive a number from mailbox, add 1 and output it.
message.context: The task creates mailbox and sends a message in another parallel branch. Obtain the value by receiving the message.
message.hint: Use ? to receive from mailbox, give the received value a name, then calculate the output.

join.title: Waiting for two messages
join.goal: Jointly receive the messages from west and east, then output their sum.
join.context: The task sends two numeric reports in separate branches. Both values must contribute to the result.
join.hint: Put both receive conditions in one ? receive expression, joined by &, then add the values in its body.

coordination.title: Coordinating a dispatch
coordination.goal: Jointly receive west and east, then call a function to total them. Add reserve if the total is greater than threshold; otherwise output the total itself.
coordination.context: The task supplies threshold, reserve and two channels. Numeric reports arrive as messages; calculate their total through a function.
coordination.hint: Define the total function first, then wait for both messages. Use that same total in the condition and the final output.

heist.title: Bank infiltration
heist.intro: Write a strategy that reads the patrol and brings the case out. Every decision changes a continuous run.
heist.running: Your strategy is reading the scene every 0.8 seconds.
heist.paused: Paused. Positions and active time are held.

heist.inputNote: distance and guard are signed metres from you. facing is -1 for left and 1 for right. cover says whether waiting here hides you. alarm and energy range from 0 to 100. phase ranges from 0 to 3.
heist.contract: Define decide(distance, guard, facing, cover, alarm, energy, phase). Return one action number from 1 to 6. The game calls it and displays its output; do not add another .log(). These numbers are game signals, not built-in Tolang commands.
heist.signals: The call must output exactly one number from 1 to 6.
heist.waiting: The program is waiting for a message. It has not chosen an action.

heist.artError: The characters could not load. Reload to try again.

heist.recordNote: These are personal run records. They do not certify language mastery or a ranked result.
heist.rules: Stay within 4 metres and keep using an objective to complete it. Waiting in cover hides you. Moving interrupts an unfinished action. A closed door blocks movement and sight. A patrol within 28 metres sees ahead, and physical contact catches you unless you are hidden. Sprinting spends more stamina and raises alert.
heist.hintText: Watch both distance and direction. A patrol approaching a dark alcove is different from one walking away. Let it pass before leaving cover; keep enough stamina for an escape.

rewrite.title: Make the program your own
rewrite.intro: Keep the program as a starting point. Change any part you need, run it, and explain to yourself why the signals changed.
rewrite.guide: Continue by changing a whole program
rewrite.ready: Your starting program is editable. Predict the new output before running.
rewrite.changed: The program changed. Run it again to check this version.
rewrite.success: This version meets the rewrite goal. Next, solve a new task without the starting program.
rewrite.retry: The program ran, but does not meet the goal yet. Compare the signals and follow the values through the execution.

rewrite.scope: This practice does not change your task score or mark a lesson complete.

signal.goal: Send two signals in order: 3, then 8. One line can send one signal; how will you send two?
signal.hint: Keep the first .log() call and add another. Each call displays its own value.

addition.goal: Show 10, then 13. Use addition to produce the signals; you can change both numbers in a calculation.
addition.hint: You can write more than one calculation. Keep .log() after each calculated value.

names.goal: Keep a number under a name and use it in additions that show 13, then 17.
names.hint: Use the same named value in two calculations. The numbers you add do not have to be equal.

leap.goal: Build a jump signal of 9 by adding two numbers. Change the whole expression if you want.
leap.hint: Choose two numbers whose sum is 9. Send the calculated value with .log().

comparison.goal: Show false, then true, using comparisons. You may change both sides and add a second comparison.
comparison.hint: A comparison produces a boolean. Try reversing which side holds the larger number.

branch.goal: Make a comparison choose a branch that displays 3. You can change the fuel, condition and branch contents.
branch.hint: First decide which branch runs for your fuel value. Change what that branch sends.

repeat.goal: Use a loop and add to each visited value to display 4, 6, 10. For example, visit [3, 5, 9] and add 1 to each value.
repeat.hint: Change both the list and the calculation inside the loop. The loop variable holds a different value on each visit.

counter.goal: Use a while loop to display 3, 4, 5, then stop. Set a new starting value and stopping condition.
counter.hint: Think about the first value, the last allowed value, and how the counter changes each time.

function.goal: Call a synchronous addition function twice so it displays 9, then 13. Reuse the function with different inputs.
function.hint: Keep the function definition once. Call it twice and display each returned result.

reply.goal: Use function replies and addition to produce 11, then 15. For example, add 3 to the inputs 8 and 12.
reply.hint: Change the function body and try different inputs. Keep return ! for its reply.

message.goal: Send a value through a channel, receive it and use it in an addition that displays 14. For example, send 10 and add 4 after receiving.
message.hint: The sender chooses the parcel value. Put the addition inside the receiver so it uses the received value.

join.goal: Send values on two channels, receive both together, and add them to display 17. For example, send 8 and 9.
join.hint: Keep the joined receive with &. Give each channel a value and calculate from the two received names.

coordination.goal: Send two values, receive both together, and total them in a function. Use a comparison to choose a branch that displays 20 using the total. One option: send 6 and 9; if the total exceeds 12, add 5.
coordination.hint: Trace the values in order: two messages, function result, condition, then the value displayed by the chosen branch.
